lesson.title: Beyond Orbits: The Quantum Mechanical Model of the Atom
lesson.summary: The quantum mechanical model replaces Bohr's fixed electron orbits with orbitals, three dimensional regions describing the probability of finding an electron, giving a picture of the atom that works for every element, not just hydrogen.
lesson.body:
The Bohr model correctly introduced the idea that electron energy is quantized, but its picture of electrons following neat circular paths, like tiny planets orbiting a sun, ran into trouble almost immediately once physicists looked closely at atoms with more than one electron. Through the 1920s, several discoveries reshaped how physicists thought about matter at this scale. Louis de Broglie proposed that particles like electrons have wave-like properties, not just particle-like ones. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle showed that it is fundamentally impossible to know both the exact position and exact momentum of an electron at the same time. Together these ideas made clear that an electron simply cannot be tracked along a precise orbit the way Bohr had imagined.

In 1926, Erwin Schrodinger built a mathematical framework, now called quantum mechanics, that treats the electron as a wave described by a wave function, usually written as the Greek letter psi. The wave function itself is not directly observable, but its square, |psi|^2, gives the probability of finding the electron at a particular point in space around the nucleus. This is the key conceptual shift from the Bohr model: instead of a definite orbit, an electron is described by an orbital, a three dimensional region of space where there is a high probability, often defined as 90 percent, of locating the electron at any given instant.

The distinction between an orbit and an orbital is more than wordplay, and it is worth stating plainly. An orbit, in the Bohr sense, is a fixed path with a definite radius that an electron is imagined to travel along, similar to a planet's path around the sun. An orbital, in the quantum mechanical sense, is a fuzzy, cloud-like region of probability with no sharp boundary and no definite path; the electron does not travel a traceable route within it, and asking exactly where the electron is at a given moment is not even a meaningful question under this model. Orbitals come in distinct three dimensional shapes, such as the spherical shape of an s orbital or the dumbbell shape of a p orbital, and these shapes come directly out of solving Schrodinger's equation for the hydrogen atom.

Unlike the Bohr model, which only produced accurate results for hydrogen, the quantum mechanical model, combined with additional considerations for electron-electron repulsion, successfully describes atoms of every element, which is why it remains the accepted model of the atom today. It keeps the piece of Bohr's model that was correct, quantized electron energy, while replacing the piece that was wrong, the idea of a fixed, knowable path.

This model is also the framework that gives rise to the modern description of electron organization within an atom. The quantized energies predicted by the model correspond to specific energy levels, and each energy level contains one or more orbitals with characteristic shapes and orientations. Understanding those energy levels in more detail, and the quantum numbers used to label them, is the natural next step built directly on this quantum mechanical foundation.
